title: Predictive Structure Behind Rare Outcomes in Random Quantum Circuits
authors: Myeongsu Kim, Travis Humble, Sabre Kais
abstract: Rare outputs of random quantum circuits are usually treated as terminal statistics. We ask whether they reveal intermediate organization that remains useful beyond the selecting future. Comparing unconditioned random-normal (RN) and peak-selected random-peaked (RP) circuits from the same local generator, we find stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution but reduced bipartite and output spreading in RP across n=8-16. Exact full-suffix decomposition reveals stronger peak-directed interference. The structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across four nominal depths at n=8-14, with 2.01-7.15 fold RP enrichment in the depth extensions at fixed, independently calibrated thresholds. Within the unconditioned ensemble, a structural prefix score predicts fresh-event probability without using the evaluated circuits' terminal outcomes. Population-preserving phase scrambling identifies a functional contribution from relative-phase organization across the tested settings, including primary-depth held-out confirmation. RP trajectory-guided initialization improves high-peak yield over Haar initialization under common local refinement. Intermediate multivariate guidance also improves the fresh-continuation susceptibility of constructed states beyond peak-only guidance across the same size-depth grid. Rare outputs thus reveal intermediate physical organization that remains useful under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction.
summary: This work analyzes random quantum circuits to determine if rare measurement outcomes encode useful information about the circuit's intermediate dynamics. By comparing peak-selected circuits to random ones, the authors demonstrate that these rare events reveal a persistent, quantifiable structural organization. This finding suggests that quantum measurement can guide future quantum operations, offering a new principle for quantum circuit design.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether rare, high-probability outputs observed in random quantum circuits contain predictive structural information useful for guiding subsequent quantum evolution.
main_result: Rare outputs reveal intermediate physical organization that is useful for guiding circuit construction, showing a measurable 'fresh-future advantage' when comparing peak-selected circuits to random ones.
method: The authors compare statistics from Random-Normal (RN) and Peak-Selected (RP) random quantum circuits, employing structural observables and developing predictive prefix scores.
model_or_system: The model uses open one-dimensional brickwall quantum circuits generated by Haar-U(4) nearest-neighbor gates, analyzed across varying system sizes and depths.
key_observables: Quantum Mutual Information (IQ), Normalized Cut Entanglement (Ec), Normalized Shannon Entropy (eH1), and the peak-amplification functional ($\Gamma_{	ext{peak}}$).
important_parameters: System sizes $n=8-16$ and multiple nominal circuit depths ($\delta=0, 1, 2, 3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across different nominal depths, even if the terminal unitary distribution is fixed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the persistence of the 'fresh-future function' across added depth settings, showing quantitative ratios (RP/RN) and phase interaction effects.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the problem (rare outcomes), developing comparative metrics (RN vs RP), quantifying structural advantages (prefix scores, phase scrambling), and concluding with applications to circuit construction.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for extracting non-terminal, predictive structure from complex quantum measurements, which is crucial for designing efficient quantum algorithms.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Peak-conditioned circuits separate from their parent ensemble throughout the pre-output trajectory. Cohort means and circuit-bootstrap 95% intervals are shown for 1000 RN and 1000 RP circuits at n = 14. The horizontal coordinate is physical depth divided by n. The dotted line marks the total depth L/n = 1.5; the terminal checkpoint itself is excluded. Panels show (a) all-pair quantum mutual information, (b) full-distribution L1 redistribution, (c) normalized cut-entanglement deficit, and (d) normalized output-entropy deficit. Panels (a), (c), and (d) use logarithmic axes.

FIG. 2. The RN–RP structural signature persists across the tested sizes. Hedges-g effects and 95% ensemble-stratified circuit-bootstrap intervals are shown for the four trajectory endpoints. Blue points denote n = 8–14 core cohorts and orange points the frozen 110-RN/110-RP extension at n = 16. The effects retain their directions but are not monotone in n, supporting finite-size transport rather than an asymptotic scaling claim.

FIG. 3. RP trajectories exhibit greater and more peak-directed quantum interference. (a) A representative exact full-suffix Iabs(t) trajectory at n = 14, shown for visual clarity, with lines denoting cohort means and bands circuit-bootstrap 95% intervals. The dashed line marks the fixed analysis cut t∗/n = 1. (b) Fixed-cut Hedges effects for Iabs across n = 8–16. (c) Circuit-level signed peak-output interference fraction F peak t∗ on a logarithmic axis. The peak output is defined retrospectively from each coherent final distribution.

FIG. 4. Peak-selected states retain enhanced susceptibility after continuation replacement. Original continuations are discarded before RN and RP receive common fresh banks, evaluated at the calibrated thresholds γn in Table III. (a) Event probabilities remain separated. (b) Risk differences are positive at every size and after equal weighting across n = 8, 10, 12, 14. All displayed intervals are 95% intervals obtained by resampling the state and continuation axes while preserving shared-bank pairing.

FIG. 5. Intermediate-state structure predicts peak probability under regenerated continuations. The unconditional cohorts at n = 8, 10, 12, 14 are evaluated at the calibrated thresholds γn in Table III. (a) Independently drawn shared banks give concordant frozen prefix-score slopes. (b) The slope is positive at every core size, with the across-size estimate (equal weight per size) shown by the dashed line and band. (c) Fresh-continuation event probabilities separate the upper and lower score quartiles. All displayed intervals are 95% intervals obtained by resampling the state and continuation axes while preserving shared-bank pairing.
